links.note: 181 says that even of a man who does not speak of virtue and does wrong (அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும்), it is pleasing to hear 'he does not backbite'. 150 uses the same frame, அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும், and says it is good that he not desire another man's wife. The pairing shows the book using one formula to mark two abstentions as a floor that still counts in a person who has otherwise let virtue go.

181 holds that not backbiting is still good in a man who otherwise does wrong (அல்ல செயினும் ... இனிது). 297 says that if one keeps to not lying, not doing the other virtues is good (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று). Both single out one restraint of speech and weigh it against the whole of the rest of conduct, though 297 goes further and treats it as sufficient.

182 condemns running a person down behind his back and then smiling falsely at him (புறனழீஇப் பொய்த்து நகை). 824 warns one to fear the deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை). The false smile is judged from the doer's side in the Book of Virtue and from the victim's side in the chapter on false friendship.

182 calls it worse than denying virtue to slander someone when absent and smile at him when present. 820 tells one not to come near those who are friendly in the house and blame you in the assembly (மனைக்கெழீஇ மன்றில் பழிப்பார்). 820 turns the moral verdict of 182 into practical advice about which friendships to refuse.

183 says that dying yields more of the gain the books of virtue speak of than living by backbiting and falsehood (பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்). 967 says that rather than live by following those who scorn you (வாழ்தலின்), it is better to be called ruined as you are. Both use the comparative 'than living thus' to say that a kind of life can cost more than its end, once for the slanderer's two faces and once for lost honour.

183 ranks death above a life kept up by backbiting and pretence. 230 says nothing is more bitter than death (சாதலின் இன்னாத தில்லை), yet even it is sweet when one cannot give. Each verse measures a fault or lack by setting death beside it and finding death the better; the pairing shows how the book uses that comparison for both a wrong done and a good left undone.

184 concedes speaking without kindly regard to a person's face (கண்ணின்று கண்ணறச் சொல்லினும்) and forbids only the word said in his absence that does not look to what follows (முன்னின்று பின்நோக்காச் சொல்). 795 goes further and tells one to seek out friends able to speak so that one weeps and to rebuke (அழச்சொல்லி ... இடித்து). What 184 merely tolerates, hard speech face to face, 795 treats as a mark of the friend worth choosing.

184: though you speak harshly to his face (சொல்லினும்), do not speak (சொல்லற்க) the heedless word behind his back. 197: let the worthy say what lacks நயன் if they must (சொல்லினுஞ் சொல்லுக), it is good that they not say what lacks use. The two neighbouring chapters use the same concessive move, granting a lesser fault of speech in order to isolate the one the chapter is about.

185 says that a man's heart does not really speak virtue is seen from the meanness of his backbiting (புறஞ்சொல்லும் புன்மையாற் காணப்படும்). 193 says that expansive talk of useless things itself declares the speaker to be without நயன் (நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும்). In both a kind of speech is treated as evidence about the speaker, whatever he professes.

34 says that being spotless in the mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noise (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் ... ஆகுல நீர பிற). 185 applies this to a case: a man may say virtue is good, but his backbiting shows it is not said from the heart (அறஞ்சொல்லும் நெஞ்சத்தான் அன்மை). 185 gives a test by which the outward show that 34 dismisses can be detected.

185 reads a man's inner lack of virtue from his backbiting. 959 says that as the sprout shows what lies in the soil, the words of the mouth show the family one is born in (காட்டும் குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல்). Both treat speech as the visible sign of something hidden, the heart in one case and lineage in the other.

186 says the one who tells another's blame (பிறன்பழி கூறுவான்) will have his own faults sorted through and told (தன்பழியுள்ளும் திறன்தெரிந்து கூறப்படும்). 319 says that hurt done to others in the forenoon comes back on oneself in the afternoon (பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்). The same return of the deed appears for speech and for injury; in 186 the return is carried out by other people's tongues.

186 warns the teller of others' faults that his own will be told. 980 says greatness covers another's weakness while smallness only tells faults (சிறுமைதான் குற்றமே கூறிவிடும்). 186 gives the consequence of the habit and 980 gives its diagnosis: fault-telling is what smallness does.

187 says those who do not know how to make friends by words that bring laughter (நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர்) will part even their own kin by words that divide (பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்). 525 says one who can give and speak pleasantly will be surrounded by kin in layers (இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் ... சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). The two state the same link between speech and keeping one's people, from its negative and positive sides, in the Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth.

187 treats speaking so that others laugh (நகச்சொல்லி) as the way friendship is made. 784 says friendship is not for laughing (நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல்) but for going ahead to rebuke when the friend oversteps. 784 limits 187: pleasant talk may begin a friendship, but it is not what the friendship is for.

187 blames those who divide their own kin by divisive talk (கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்). 633 lists dividing (பிரித்தல்) among a minister's abilities, together with keeping his own side and rejoining those who have parted; Parimelazhagar takes the dividing to be of the enemy's allies. The same act is a fault when turned on one's own people and a skill of statecraft when turned on opponents.

188 asks what those whose way is to spread even the faults of people close to them (துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும்) would do to strangers (என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு). In 1165 the woman asks what those who can bring grief within friendship (நட்பினுள்) would become in enmity. Both argue from conduct toward intimates to what must follow toward others; in 1165 it is a lover's complaint, not a general teaching.

188 describes people whose habit is to broadcast (தூற்றும்) the faults of those near them. 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum because they carry any secret they have heard to others (கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான்). 1076 places the habit of 188 in the Kural's portrait of the base person.

151 makes the earth that holds up those who dig into it (அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்) the model of bearing with those who scorn you. 189 asks whether it is with an eye to virtue that the earth bears the weight (பொறை) of the man who watches for someone's absence to speak mean words. 189 turns the earlier image on the backbiter: he is carried only because the earth is forbearing; Parimelazhagar reads it as the earth taking this bearing to be its virtue.

189 speaks of the backbiter as a weight the earth bears (வையம் ... பொறை). 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (நிலக்குப் பொறை). The figure of a person as dead weight on the ground is used in both for someone who fails others in ordinary dealings, by malicious speech in one and by lack of regard in the other.

189 wonders that the earth bears the backbiter's weight at all. 990 says that if the worthy decline in worth, the great earth will not bear its load (இருநிலந்தான் தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை). Together they show the image used at both ends: the earth strains under the bad man, and is able to carry its load only while the worthy stay worthy.

190 asks what harm could come to living beings if people saw their own faults as they see those of strangers (தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்). 436 asks what fault could attach to a ruler who first removes his own fault and then looks at others' (தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்). Both use the same conditional காண்கிற்பின் and the same order of self before others, as an ethic for everyone and as a rule for the king who must judge.

190 wishes that people would see their own faults as they see a stranger's. 930 asks whether a drinker, when sober and seeing another man drunk, does not think of his own lapse when he drinks (உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு). 930 is a concrete instance of the failure 190 names: the other man's fault is seen clearly and one's own identical fault is not.

no_link_reason: The verse states a plain consequence (irritating many, despised by all); candidates outside the chapter share only the topic of speech before others.
Its comparison of useless talk before many with unwelcome acts toward friends has no real counterpart elsewhere; nearby candidates only repeat the chapter's topic.

links.note: 193 says that a man's spreading out useless matter in speech itself announces that he is without நயன் (நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும்). 959 says the words of the mouth show the family one comes from, as a sprout shows the soil. In both the speech testifies about the speaker; 193 makes the talk itself the subject of the verb 'says', which Parimelazhagar notes.

97 says the word that yields use and does not part from good quality (பயன்ஈன்று பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல்) produces நயன் and brings good (நயன் ஈன்று நன்றி பயக்கும்). 194 says words without use and without quality (பயன்சாராப் பண்பில்சொல்), spoken among many, are without நயன் and remove one from good (நயன்சாரா நன்மையின் நீக்கும்). The four terms பயன், பண்பு, நயன் and நன்மை/நன்றி recur in the same roles, so 194 reads as the negative image of 97.

195 says that if people of fine nature (நீர்மையுடையார்) speak useless things, their distinction and the regard it earned leave them. 965 says even those like a hill will sink if they do a lowering thing the size of a kunri seed. Both hold that standing does not protect the eminent from a small lapse; 195 applies this to idle speech.

195 says useless talk costs people of fine nature their distinction (சீர்மை சிறப்பொடு நீங்கும்). 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து). 957 supplies a reason for 195: a fault that would pass unnoticed in others is conspicuous in those held high.

196 says not to call the man who keeps up useless talk a man (மகன் எனல்) but chaff among people (மக்கட் பதடி). 1071 says the base look just like human beings (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்). Both separate the human form from being fully a person; 196 gives one specific ground for the distinction, and Parimelazhagar explains the chaff as lacking the kernel of understanding.

196 calls the habitual idle talker chaff, a husk with nothing in it. 406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist and are like barren saline land that yields nothing (பயவாக் களரனையர்). Both take a farming image of something that looks like the useful thing and gives no yield, and both turn on பயன், what a person produces.

197 lets the worthy say even what lacks நயன் but holds that they should not say what lacks use (பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று). 697 tells one who serves a king to say what is wanted and never to say what is without use even if asked (வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்); Parimelazhagar glosses வினையில as matters without benefit. The rule against useless speech is kept as firmly at court as in private ethics, and neither verse lets circumstances excuse it.

193 says that useless talk at length shows the speaker to be without நயன், so the two faults go together. 197 separates them and ranks them: speech without நயன் may be let pass in the worthy, speech without use may not. Read together, 197 makes uselessness the graver of the two; Parimelazhagar draws the same ranking from சொல்லினும்.

no_link_reason: The claim that those who examine rare ends say only what has great use is echoed only loosely in the chapters on eloquence; nothing specific enough to teach by pairing.

links.note: 199 says those of stainless sight, freed from delusion (மருள்தீர்ந்த மாசறு காட்சியவர்), do not say meaningless things even by forgetfulness. 352 uses nearly the same phrase, மருள்நீங்கி மாசறு காட்சியவர்க்கு, for those to whom darkness departs and joy comes; Parimelazhagar takes it there as the true knowledge that ends birth. The phrase that names the liberated knower in the chapter on realisation is used in 199 to describe how such a person speaks.

199: those of clear sight do not say meaningless things even in forgetfulness (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார்). 139: for those who have conduct, saying evil things with the mouth even by a slip is not possible (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் ஒல்லா). Both claim that a settled quality rules out even accidental bad speech, with knowledge as the ground in one and conduct in the other.

199 says what those of stainless sight will not say. 258 says those whose sight has parted from fault (செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார்) will not eat flesh that has parted from life. The book repeatedly states a restraint as what people of clear காட்சி simply do not do; here the same form covers speech and diet.

200 says to speak, among words, those that have use and not those that have none (சொல்லுக சொல்லிற் பயனுடைய). 645 says to speak a word after knowing there is no other word that can defeat it (சொல்லுக சொல்லைப் பிறிதோர்சொல்). Both open with சொல்லுக and play on repeated சொல்; the test for a word is use in the Book of Virtue and whether it can be beaten in the minister's chapter on eloquence.
